item.title: Barker:
item.content:encoded:
This is a short story about dogs and the things that they want, written for TyGently for the 2020 Secret Santa. There's a small reference to another Soviet dog, if you care to find it.

I know that the death is not historically accurate, but accounts have changed repeatedly over the years, so it's not completely out of the question. The record is regrettably silent on the matter of giant alien space gods and their demand for blood sacrifices, so I can't vouch for the accuracy of that aspect.

Thanks to Riemann, weizhong, and A Random Day for looking over and providing critique.

item.title: SCP-5236:
item.content:encoded:
(Zyn, do you just lurk on the Recent Posts page and leap in with relevant links/info when you see somebody asking for help, like a superhero with extremely specific priorities?)

Creidieki, one issue is that a lot of Foundation lore is ambiguous, and is interpreted different ways by different authors. "Does the black moon howl?" has been used as a motto, a passcode prompt, a key concept in an SCP-001 entry, and many more besides. The only real common thread is that it's spooky and mysterious, and somehow associated with the Foundation. Having a clear reference for this sort of thing can be a bit tricky!

I tried to write this article such that even if you're not super familiar with Foundation lore, you can pick up enough from context clues to get the gist. The Ethics Committee is exactly what it says on the tin, for example. or is it?probablyhmmmdon't worry about it.

Anyway, the Foundation can be pretty lore-dense sometimes, but I hope you still enjoyed the article!

item.title: SCP-5359: Re: Note from the author

item.title: Don't Knock on Strange Doors:
item.content:encoded:
exorbiant amounts

I think you mean "exorbitant", and there's a sentence in here that has a repeated "might". Just Ctrl+F for "might" and you'll find it. Beyond that, I think the dialogue portrayed here is a bit outside what someone would put in their seminar, I think people would rather just summarize the information that was said instead of writing out people as if they're characters. For example:

"So, what comes out of the door?" I asked, feeling the doorframe with my fingertips.

This is prose. In a summary of events, someone would probably write instead:

So I asked them what came out of the door.

Then the rest of that interaction could be summed by something like: "They told me that nothing comes out of the door, but that it opened to a dark ages cathedral in another dimension, housing a community of communist flower people."

Stuff like that. But, besides these gripes, I like this. It's cute, in a kind of way. I feel like if you followed this researcher around in episodic fashion, the tone would be that he always keeps his head, in a kind of lackadaisical sense where he doesn't ever feel too much in danger, and always safely makes it out while chaos collapses in around him. +1 because I like that tone, and the ending line got a chuckle.

This one hooked me at the start, what with the format screw and music, but as I read on, it just didn't reel me in at all. The bit about space signals and the log of someone going insane didn't really "hit", even after a second read of the article. While this definitely feels appropriately confusing for a department of miscommunications article, that alone doesn't make an article interesting or enjoyable to read. There's clear effort here, and it did do a decent job getting me to read it all the way through, but with the cons I mentioned earlier I'll be giving this a novote.

item.title: SCP-5580:
item.content:encoded:
My review from the Art Exchange forum:

This is a fantastic article about a semi-Fifthist artifact's interactions with a Viatnamese uprising against French rule in the late 1930s. It's pretty amazing how much detail the author went into, and it's extra amazing how much character he wrote in. You can feel the love for history here. It's not just an interesting conflict in its own right, but it talks about how information gets recorded in the first place, carrying a theme of "your version of the truth", between how the Japanese interacted with the rock, the American talked about his view of the Vietnamese, and how the Vietnamese viewed the struggle, all with the central thematic piece of the pink rock which is "raw power", shaped by the wants and views of those who used it. It is an intimidatingly coherent piece with clear Lovecraftian inspiration (I know, I know, you can use "cosmic horror" to avoid attributing everything to direct Lovecraft inspiration nowadays but this is even set in the 1930s, you gotta realize that that's really contributing to the Lovecraft vibe here) as I always love to see in these Fifthist pieces. Good fucking job. One of the most solid creations for this art exchange.

I don't think I have anything to add. +1

item.title: SCP-5502:
item.content:encoded:
Whoops! Ignore the first version of this comment. It was meant for someone else. Anyhow, this is a very interesting skip. I feel like a little bit of it is flying over my head, but I like the interconnectedness of it. The TV is a weird anomaly, the interaction with another anomaly is strange (I bet I'd get it more if I read the related skip), I like the "small thing creates huge implications when anomalies combine" because that's what makes most sense to me. Like, if these things work off of nonsense-logic, of course two things that seem completely safe have the potential to fuck the whole world up if you put them next to each other. That's why the Foundation is so anal about containment!

+1, if you couldn't tell, and more good Fifthist content is always appreciated.
